631.quote_or_event: In the Zafarnamah, his Persian verse letter to Emperor Aurangzeb written in 1706, Guru Gobind Singh set out when force may rightly be used. In its often-quoted verse 22 he says, in effect, that it is lawful to take up the sword only when all other means have failed. The letter judges public policy by moral principle and stresses the importance of means over ends.
631.explanation: The Zafarnamah is the nearest thing in Sikh sources to a statement of statecraft: it weighs the right means and the right moment before a grave course of action is taken.
631.tie_back: The Kural defines the minister as one who thinks through the means, the right time and the method; the Zafarnamah likewise ties a grave decision to exhausting other means and choosing the right time.
631.source: Encyclopaedia of Sikhism (Punjabi University, Patiala, ed. Harbans Singh), 'Zafarnamah', via The Sikh Encyclopedia (paraphrase)
631._accuracy_note: Next-best: Sikh scripture has no doctrine of the minister; this text concerns the ethics of resorting to force rather than a counsellor's skill, and it is preserved in the Dasam Granth, whose compilation is debated among Sikhs; it is used because nothing in the Guru Granth Sahib fits.

632.quote_or_event: In May 1675 a group of Kashmiri Pandits, persecuted under the Mughal governor of Kashmir, came to Guru Tegh Bahadur at Anandpur for help. According to the Gurbilas account cited in the Encyclopaedia of Sikhism, the Guru said that the earth's burden would be lifted only if a worthy person gave his head, and the young Gobind Das replied that none was worthier than the Guru himself. Guru Tegh Bahadur took up their cause and was executed in Delhi later that year.
632.explanation: Sikhs remember Guru Tegh Bahadur as one who gave his life to protect the freedom of conscience of people who were not even of his own faith.
632.tie_back: Among a minister's qualities the Kural lists firm courage and the protection of the people; Guru Tegh Bahadur's martyrdom is the Sikh model of fearless protection of the vulnerable.
632.source: Encyclopaedia of Sikhism (Punjabi University, Patiala, ed. Harbans Singh), 'Tegh Bahadur, Guru', via The Sikh Encyclopedia (paraphrase)
632._accuracy_note: Next-best: it illustrates courage and protecting the people, two of the Kural's qualities, but a Guru giving his life is not a minister serving a king, and learning and sustained effort are not covered; the dialogue comes from an 18th-century Gurbilas text quoted by the encyclopedia.

633.quote_or_event: During the long siege of Anandpur a band of Sikhs disowned Guru Gobind Singh and deserted him. Later, repentant, they returned and died fighting for him at Khidrana on 29 December 1705. The Guru tore up their written disclaimer and blessed them as the Chali Mukte, the Forty Liberated Ones, and the place became Muktsar.
633.explanation: The Chali Mukte are remembered daily in the Sikh Ardas; their story is one of estranged followers taken back and honoured rather than rejected.
633.tie_back: The Kural prizes the minister who can bring back those who have broken away; Guru Gobind Singh received the deserters back and erased the record of their desertion.
633.source: Encyclopaedia of Sikhism (Punjabi University, Patiala, ed. Harbans Singh), 'Chali Mukte', via The Sikh Encyclopedia (paraphrase)
633._accuracy_note: Reasonable fit for the third skill, reconciling those who left; it is the Guru's forgiveness rather than a minister's diplomacy, and it says nothing of detaching the enemy's allies or keeping one's own side loyal.

634.quote_or_event: “Wisdom leads us to serve our Lord and Master; through wisdom, honor is obtained.”
634.explanation: In a salok of Saarang ki Vaar, Guru Nanak praises akal, practical wisdom and discernment, as what guides right action and earns honour.
634.tie_back: The Kural wants the minister to understand a matter, act after careful choice and state his conclusion firmly; Guru Nanak likewise makes discerning wisdom the guide of right action.
634.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1245, Raag Saarang (Saarang ki Vaar, salok), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
634._accuracy_note: Next-best: it praises discernment in general but names none of the Kural's three specific abilities, and the wisdom it means is directed to serving God rather than to counsel in affairs of state.

635.quote_or_event: “O Baba, speak only that which will bring you honor.”
635.explanation: In a hymn of Siree Raag, Guru Nanak urges that speech be weighed, so that one says only what is worthy and brings honour.
635.tie_back: The Kural wants as a counsellor one whose speech is measured and full of learning; Guru Nanak likewise asks for speech that is weighed and worthy.
635.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 15, Siree Raag, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
635._accuracy_note: Next-best: it matches only the measured-speech element; knowing what is right and knowing how things are done are not addressed, and the honour meant is honour before God.

636.quote_or_event: “Contemplate and reflect upon knowledge, and you will become a benefactor to others.”
636.explanation: In a hymn of Raag Aasaa, Guru Nanak says that learning becomes valuable only when it is reflected on and inwardly understood, and so put to the service of others.
636.tie_back: The Kural says no scheme can stand against someone who joins native sharpness to book learning; Guru Nanak likewise asks that learning be joined to one's own reflection.
636.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 356, Raag Aasaa, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
636._accuracy_note: Next-best: both join learning to inner understanding, but Guru Nanak's goal is benefiting others, not outwitting stratagems, and he does not speak of natural acuteness as such.

637.quote_or_event: “You may read and read loads of books; you may read and study vast multitudes of books. … O Nanak, only one thing is of any account: everything else is useless babbling and idle talk in ego.”
637.explanation: In a famous salok of Asa di Vaar, Guru Nanak says that mountains of book learning count for little unless they lead to what truly matters.
637.tie_back: The Kural tells the minister to know how the world actually works as well as what the books say; Guru Nanak likewise refuses to treat book learning as enough by itself.
637.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 467, Raag Aasaa (Asa di Vaar, salok), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
637._accuracy_note: Next-best: both say book learning is not enough, but the Kural adds knowledge of worldly affairs, whereas Guru Nanak points beyond the world to the one thing that counts, God's Name.

638.quote_or_event: “Nanak speaks the Word of Truth; he proclaims the Truth at this, the right time.”
638.explanation: This line closes a hymn of Raag Tilang that belongs to Guru Nanak's Babarvani, his hymns about Babur's invasion, in which he speaks plainly of the cruelty of the powerful.
638.tie_back: The Kural says the one who stands beside the king must still tell him what is truly good, even if the king rejects advice; Guru Nanak insists on proclaiming the truth to the powerful at the very moment it is needed.
638.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 723, Raag Tilang, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
638._accuracy_note: Reasonable but partial: it shares the duty of speaking truth to power, but Guru Nanak speaks as a prophet addressing an age, not as a counsellor advising his own king.

639.quote_or_event: When Guru Gobind Singh's family was scattered after leaving Anandpur in December 1705, their own cook, Gangu, took the Guru's mother Mata Gujari and his two youngest sons to his house at Kheri. Tempted by the money in their saddlebag, he stole it and betrayed them to the Mughal officials at Morinda. The children were later executed at Sirhind.
639.explanation: Sikh memory holds up Gangu, a trusted member of the household, as the type of the betrayer from within, whose treachery did more harm than the Mughal army that had failed to take them.
639.tie_back: The Kural says one treacherous minister at your side is worse than seventy crores of open enemies; the betrayal of the Guru's family by their own household servant is Sikh history's starkest example.
639.source: Encyclopaedia of Sikhism (Punjabi University, Patiala, ed. Harbans Singh), 'Sahibzada Zorawar Singh', via The Sikh Encyclopedia (paraphrase)
639._accuracy_note: Strong thematic fit on betrayal from within one's own household; Gangu was a cook, not a minister, and the comparison with the outer army is an interpretive gloss, not stated by the source.

640.quote_or_event: “We are good at talking, but our actions are bad.”
640.explanation: In a salok of Siree Raag ki Vaar, Guru Nanak confesses the gap between fine words and the deeds that should follow them.
640.tie_back: The Kural says those without the skill to carry things through leave their work unfinished even after good planning; Guru Nanak likewise names the gap between fine words and actual deeds.
640.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 85, Siree Raag (Siree Raag ki Vaar, salok), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
640._accuracy_note: Next-best: both contrast good intentions with failed execution, but Guru Nanak speaks of moral conduct and inner impurity, not of a lack of executive skill in carrying out planned work.
